s: Chapter 2: Tool Design and MCP Integration
Let's open with a story.
It's a busy Monday on a customer support desk.
The desk is run by an agent.
Somewhere behind the scenes, the order database starts timing out.
And every time the agent asks for a customer's orders, the tool quietly hands back an empty list.
What does the agent do?
Exactly what you would do if you believed that list.
It tells customer after customer that they have no orders on file.
And it cheerfully offers to open a new account for each of them.
Dozens of people hear this before anyone notices.
So what went wrong?
Nothing was wrong with the model.
Nothing was wrong with the prompt.
The tool told a lie by staying silent.
And the agent believed it.
Why?
Because the tool is the only window the agent has onto your systems.
That's what this chapter is about.
Domain two is Tool Design and Model Context Protocol Integration.
It carries eighteen percent of the exam.
So roughly one question in six.
The idea underneath the whole domain is simple to say, and easy to forget.
The model cannot see your database.
It cannot read your source code.
It cannot ask a colleague what a field means.
So what does it see?
Four things.
A tool's name.
A written description.
A list of parameters, each carrying its own description.
And whatever comes back when it calls.
That's its whole world at the moment of choosing.
There's no side channel.
And no second opinion.
So tool design is architecture, not plumbing.
A vague description produces a wrong call.
A raw data dump clogs the model's working memory.
A permission failure flattened into a generic "try again" produces an agent that retries forever.
Here's the catch.
None of those look like tool bugs during triage.
They look like model failures.
And teams swap models for weeks, when the defect sits in a forty-word description.
Now, how does the exam test this domain?
Hold on to this, because it applies to every question that follows.
You'll be handed a system that works, but is degrading.
And you'll be asked which structural change fixes the root cause.
The best answer changes the contract.
That means the description, the schema, the error payload, the tool set, the configuration scope, or the kind of capability the server exposes.
The best answer almost never rewords a prompt.
And the distractors?
They're real fixes, aimed at symptoms.
A prompt rule for a bad description.
A retry for a denial.
A forcing setting for too many tools.
A new subagent for what is really a wording problem.
Here's the plan.
We'll go through the five official task statements, in order.
Part one.
Designing tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries.
Part two.
Structured error responses.
Part three.
Distributing tools across agents, and configuring tool choice.
Part four.
Integrating Model Context Protocol servers into Claude Code and agent workflows.
From now on, I'll call that M C P.
Part five.
Choosing and using the built-in tools well.
Then a rapid trap round.
And a closing recap of ten things to remember.
